name: Femi Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Femi. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and also what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior buyer for Greenway Produce, a fruit and vegetable wholesaler at the city's wholesale market. We buy from growers and importers and sell on to restaurants and greengrocers. I'm at the market by four in the morning, walking the stalls, tasting tomatoes, squeezing avocados, and then by nine I'm at the laptop with an AI tool comparing prices and forecasting what the restaurants will want next week. I love the early mornings, and I hate the waste when we get the forecast wrong and a pallet of strawberries goes soft.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did the AI tool come in at Greenway?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I brought it in, honestly. The owner, Mr Okoro, is sixty and runs everything from a notebook, and I showed him the tool could tell us which restaurants over-order on Fridays. He let me keep using it, but he still pays me less than the other buyers because I'm junior and I still make rookie mistakes. My partner Zainab is a teaching assistant, and between us we've got about three weeks of money saved, which isn't much in a job where the market can be quiet in January.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five short pictures of the future. The first is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are good but they're not a revolution, which is what I've seen anyway. At the market I'd tell the older traders they can relax. Online I'd probably share my own little tricks, how I use it for forecasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit disappointed, because I was betting on AI to help me jump ahead. My job is safe, but my pay is still low and Greenway's margins are tiny. January is always scary for us, when restaurants are quiet and Mr Okoro cuts hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools every day and try to cut our waste, because if I can show Mr Okoro I saved him money, I can ask for more. I'd keep a little cash aside for January. And I'd keep learning the produce itself, which is what the old buyers really know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty steady, but the January worry is always there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much waste could you cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last summer Greenway threw out maybe forty boxes of soft fruit a week. If I can get that down to twenty, that's real money. I'd put it in a spreadsheet and show him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to you in a quiet January?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year I lost two days a week for six weeks. Zainab covered the rent, and I felt rubbish about it. I did some delivery driving to fill in.

Online I'd share my own **forecasting tricks**.

Quiet **Januarys** are always scary, when the owner cuts hours.
do: Use AI to **cut waste** and show Mr Okoro the savings.
Keep a little cash aside for **January**.
Keep learning the **produce itself** from the older buyers.
feel: Pretty **steady**, with the **January worry** always there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good for people who learn fast and hard for people who don't, so learn fast. At work I'd offer to set up the new systems. Online I'd say firms should pay for training, but workers should take it seriously too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm one of the lucky ones. My job is half hands-on, walking the market and checking quality, and robots won't squeeze an avocado for a while. The screen half gets automated, but I'm the one at Greenway who knows how to run that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Okoro to let me set up the AI ordering for all the restaurant accounts, and ask for a raise if it works. I'd start a small side thing, maybe a weekly price newsletter for greengrocers, using the AI to write it. And I'd still keep some money aside, because things can turn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly, with a bit of nerves underneath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Greenway would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Linda, who takes the restaurant orders by phone. That's exactly the customer side the AI takes. She's been there fifteen years and doesn't use email much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're excited, but your savings are thin. Doesn't that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, a bit. If Mr Okoro decided the software could do my screen work and the market work could be done by him, I'd be stuck. But I think I'm more useful than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and people need to stop pretending it isn't. At the market I'd tell people to start thinking now. I'd want the government to help small firms like Greenway, not just big ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the buying side of my job is gone by 2028, and so is my edge with the tools, because everyone has the same AI. What's left is the hands-on market work, which lasts until about 2031. For three years my value would be my nose and my hands, not the laptop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on the market side: learn from the oldest traders, get known by the growers, be the person who can tell a good mango by touch. I'd look at starting my own small wholesale round with a van, buying direct from growers for a few restaurants, because thinking AI helps a tiny business as much as a big one. Zainab and I would cut back hard to save for the van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but more pumped than scared. It's a race, and I'm quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the van and the start cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A used van is maybe five thousand, which we don't have. I'd ask my uncle for a loan and pay it back from the first year. It's a risk, but staying put is a risk too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about around 2031, when robots can do the hands-on part?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then my business has to be about the relationships, the growers who trust me. I don't know if that's enough. I'd be thirty-two and maybe starting again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a real warning, so use it. I'd tell the younger lads at the market to learn the trade and the tools both. I'd probably post about how small businesses can get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is good for me. I could stay at Greenway two or three years, get better, save properly, then go out on my own before 2031. The market side lasts until about 2034, which is time to build a proper round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd ask Mr Okoro for a raise based on the waste savings, and put all of it into a van fund. I'd start a small Saturday round with a borrowed van to test it. And I'd keep using the AI for my own forecasting so the round doesn't waste stock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, a bit nervous. Like the first day of something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Zainab about the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years of tight living and then the produce round is ours. My partner Zainab is careful with money, so she'd want a spreadsheet. She'd get one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Mr Okoro saw your Saturday round as competition?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him first, and only sell to places Greenway doesn't. He's old school but fair. Maybe he'd even want to partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so plan properly and don't panic. I'd tell people at the market it's time to learn, not to worry. Online I'd share what I'm doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years could make me. I'd get good, save, start the round, and by 2036 have a small business with a couple of vans. Robots for the hands-on side wouldn't come till about 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd focus on getting really good at buying and building trust with growers. I'd save a bit every month, even small. I'd take a short business course at the college in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful. A bit worried about money in the short term, like always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bigger firms with better AI could undercut me. That's the real risk. I'd have to be the one growers like dealing with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would success look like in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two vans, one driver, and my partner Zainab not worrying about the rent. That's what success in 2036 looks like. Maybe a kid by then.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be starting a business with no money in a hurry. What would help is small business loans for people without savings, and help for small firms to get the same AI tools as the big ones.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the market itself. If buyers and robots take over, the wholesale market where I learned everything might close. Places like that teach people a trade.
